facts.text: Severe renal impairment (eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m²).
facts.population: Patients with eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m²

facts.text: Acute or chronic metabolic acidosis, including diabetic ketoacidosis.
facts.population: Patients with metabolic acidosis or DKA

facts.text: History of serious hypersensitivity reaction to sitagliptin, metformin, or any excipients (e.g., anaphylaxis, angioedema).
facts.population: Patients with prior severe hypersensitivity to the drug or its components

facts.text: Metformin‑associated lactic acidosis (MALA) can be fatal; risk factors include renal impairment, age ≥ 65 years, contrast imaging, surgery, hypoxic states, excessive alcohol, hepatic impairment, and concomitant drugs that reduce metformin clearance.
facts.population: All patients, especially those with listed risk factors

facts.text: Pancreatitis has been reported; discontinue metformin if pancreatitis is suspected.
facts.population: Patients with signs or symptoms of acute pancreatitis

facts.text: Heart‑failure exacerbation may occur; monitor for signs and symptoms and consider discontinuation if heart failure develops.
facts.population: Patients with known or risk factors for heart failure

facts.text: Acute renal failure, sometimes requiring dialysis, has been reported; assess renal function before initiation and at least annually.
facts.population: All patients, with more frequent monitoring in the elderly or those at risk

facts.text: Long‑term metformin use may lower vitamin B12 levels; measure B12 every 2–3 years (annually for hematologic parameters).
Increased risk of hypoglycemia when combined with insulin or insulin secretagogues; dose reduction of the co‑administered agent may be required.
Serious hypersensitivity reactions (anaphylaxis, angioedema, Stevens‑Johnson syndrome) have been reported; stop drug immediately if suspected.
Severe disabling arthralgia and bullous pemphigoid have been reported; consider drug as cause and discontinue if appropriate.
facts.population: Patients developing severe joint pain or blistering skin lesions

facts.text: Take ZITUVIMET (metformin/sitagliptin fixed‑dose) orally twice daily with meals; do not split tablets.
Maximum daily dose: 100 mg sitagliptin + 2000 mg metformin HCl.
Starting dose for metformin‑naïve patients: 50 mg sitagliptin + 500 mg metformin HCl twice daily, with gradual titration to improve GI tolerance.
Starting dose for patients already on metformin: 50 mg sitagliptin twice daily plus the patient’s current metformin dose (e.g., 850 mg metformin BID → 1000 mg metformin BID).
Assess eGFR before initiation; contraindicated if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²; not recommended if eGFR 30‑<45 mL/min/1.73 m² because sitagliptin dose cannot be reduced.

Discontinue ZITUVIMET at the time of, or prior to, iodinated contrast imaging in patients with eGFR 30‑60 mL/min/1.73 m², or with liver disease, alcoholism, or heart failure; re‑evaluate eGFR 48 h after procedure before restarting.
Elderly patients (≥65 years) should start at the low end of the dosing range and have renal function monitored more frequently due to higher risk of lactic acidosis.
No overall safety or efficacy differences observed for sitagliptin in patients ≥65 years; insufficient data for metformin alone.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., topiramate, zonisamide, acetazolamide, dichlorphenamide) may increase risk of lactic acidosis; consider more frequent monitoring.

Drugs that reduce metformin clearance via OCT2/MATE inhibition (e.g., ranolazine, vandetanib, dolutegravir, cimetidine) may increase metformin exposure and lactic‑acidosis risk; evaluate benefit‑risk.
Alcohol potentiates metformin’s effect on lactate metabolism; advise patients to avoid excessive alcohol intake.
Co‑administration with insulin or insulin secretagogues increases hypoglycemia risk; dose reduction of the insulin/secretagogue may be needed.

Drugs that affect glycemic control (e.g., thiazides, corticosteroids, phenothiazines, thyroid products, estrogens, oral contraceptives, phenytoin, nicotinic acid, sympathomimetics, calcium‑channel blockers, isoniazid) may cause hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia when added or withdrawn; monitor glucose closely.
facts.population: Patients receiving any of these agents

facts.text: Metformin is primarily excreted unchanged by the kidneys; accumulation and lactic‑acidosis risk rise as renal function declines.
facts.population: All patients, especially those with impaired renal function

facts.text: Renal function (eGFR) should be assessed before starting therapy and at least annually; more frequent monitoring in elderly or patients at risk for renal decline.
If acute renal failure or significant eGFR decline occurs, discontinue metformin immediately.
